text: The 2019 Rugby World Cup (Japanese: ラグビーワールドカップ2019) was the ninth edition of the quadrennial men's rugby union world championship, hosted in Japan from 20 September to 2 November across 12 venues nationwide. The opening match was held at Ajinomoto Stadium in Chōfu, Tokyo, and the final took place at International Stadium Yokohama in Yokohama. This marked the first time the tournament was held in Asia and outside the traditional Tier 1 rugby nations. The event saw the first match cancellations due to Typhoon Hagibis, which affected three matches because of safety concerns. South Africa defeated England 32–12 in the final to win their third title, matching New Zealand's record and becoming the first team to claim the title after losing a pool-stage match. The defending champions, New Zealand, finished third after defeating Wales in the bronze final. The International Rugby Board (IRB), later renamed World Rugby, invited nations to express interest in hosting the 2015 and 2019 tournaments by 15 August 2008, with 10 unions responding and nine showing interest in the 2019 event. Russia initially bid for both tournaments but withdrew in February 2009 to focus on the 2013 Rugby World Cup Sevens; Australia withdrew on 6 May 2009. The three potential hosts—Italy, Japan, and South Africa—were announced on 8 May 2009. On 28 July 2009, the IRB confirmed England as hosts for 2015 and Japan for 2019, approved by Rugby World Cup Ltd with a 16–10 vote. From late 2013, the IRB, RWC Ltd, JRFU, and Japan 2019 conducted a process of gathering expressions of interest and meeting with potential hosts. In May 2014, 22 municipal and prefectural organizations in Japan expressed interest, with formal bids due by 31 October 2014; 14 bids were received on 5 November. Hong Kong and Singapore expressed interest in hosting matches and were included in Japan's bid but were not among the 14 stadiums announced in 2014. Nissan Stadium in Yokohama and Denka Big Swan Stadium in Niigata declined to bid. The JRFU's original 2009 bid was revised, excluding Chichibunomiya Stadium in Tokyo and including the larger 50,000-seat Nagai Stadium in Osaka. East Osaka City, which took over Hanazono Rugby Stadium from Kintetsu in April 2015, submitted a joint bid with Osaka Municipality to refurbish the stadium. Kamaishi, Hamamatsu, Kyoto, Ōita, Nagasaki, and Kumamoto were not included in the bid. Hosting areas excluded were Hokushin'etsu (Hokuriku and Kōshin'etsu) and Chūgoku (including Hiroshima and Shikoku), with no Chūgoku city hosting in the 2002 FIFA World Cup, though Hiroshima hosted in the 2006 FIBA World Championship. The new National Stadium in Tokyo, built for the 2020 Summer Olympics, was initially planned as the primary venue but was scrapped and rebid in 2015 due to design criticism and rising costs, leading to its completion being delayed. As a result, the opening match was moved to Ajinomoto Stadium and the final to Nissan Stadium in Yokohama. The top three teams from the 2015 World Cup received automatic qualification, with the remaining eight spots filled through regional qualifiers, six of which came from regional groups and two via play-offs. Qualifying groups were Africa, Americas, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. The United States qualified on 1 July 2017 by defeating Canada in a two-leg match as America 1. Fiji and Tonga qualified as Oceania 1 and 2 respectively. Samoa secured the third Oceania spot by defeating Germany in a two-leg tie the following year. Uruguay qualified in January 2018 with a 10-point win over Canada as Americas 2. Romania initially qualified as Europe 1, but after complaints from Spain over ineligible players, all three—Romania, Spain, and Belgium—were penalized, resulting in Russia qualifying and Germany entering a play-off against Samoa. Namibia qualified in August 2018 by defeating Kenya in the Rugby Africa Gold Cup final. The final spot was decided in a repechage tournament in Marseille in November 2018, won by Canada after winning all three of their matches. The pool draw took place on 10 May 2017 in Kyoto, moved from its traditional December slot after the previous World Cup to allow nations more time to improve their world rankings. The seeding system from previous tournaments was retained, with the 12 automatic qualifiers from 2015 allocated based on their World Rugby Rankings on 10 May 2017. The remaining two bands were formed from the eight qualifying teams based on their previous World Cup performance. The 20 teams were seeded according to their world rankings as of that date. The draw involved randomly selecting a ball from a pot, with the first ball assigned to Pool A, the second to Pool B, the third to Pool C, and the fourth to Pool D. Each team submitted a squad of 31 players, the same as in 2015, with the deadline being 8 September, the United States being the last to reveal their squad on 6 September. World Rugby named 12 referees, seven assistant referees, and four television match officials for the 48 matches. The opening ceremony occurred at Ajinomoto Stadium in Tokyo on 20 September 2019 at 18:30 (JST), featuring a showcase of traditional and modern Japanese culture and the evolution of rugby in Japan. Richie McCaw, former All Blacks captain and 2015 World Cup winner, performed a ceremonial handover of the Webb Ellis Cup. Six jet aircraft from Japan Air Self-Defense Force's Blue Impulse aerobatic team flew over the stadium. Kiyoe Yoshioka of Ikimono-gakari performed World in Union, the official song. The tournament was officially opened by Fumihito, Prince Akishino of Japan, with World Rugby chairman Sir Bill Beaumont delivering a speech stating: "Over the next six weeks we will experience the very best of rugby and the very best of Japan as excitement sweeps this great nation. I know Japan will be the most welcoming of hosts, you are the best. The waiting is over and the stage is set. It’s now over to the teams and the fans to make this the best World Cup ever." The 20 teams were divided into four pools of five teams, each playing a single round-robin format of 10 games, with each team playing every other team in the pool once. Teams earned four points for a win, two for a draw, and zero for a loss. A bonus point was awarded for scoring four tries or for losing by seven points or fewer, with both conditions applying if both occurred. The top two teams in each pool advanced to the quarter-finals, and the top three teams qualified for the 2023 Rugby World Cup. If teams were tied on match points, the following tiebreakers applied: if three teams were tied, the criteria were applied to determine first place, then again (starting from criterion 1) to determine second place. The opening match of the tournament was Japan versus Russia in Pool A, with Japan winning 30–10. Kotaro Matsushima scored the first hat-trick by a Japanese player at a World Cup. Kirill Golosnitsky scored the first try of the tournament in the opening match after four minutes, the fastest try ever in a World Cup opening match. Two days later, Ireland defeated Scotland 27–3. On 24 September, Samoa beat Russia 34–9 in Kumagaya. Four days later, Japan defeated Ireland 19–12 in Tokyo, scoring four out of six penalties. World Rugby later admitted three of the four offside penalties were incorrectly awarded. Kenki Fukuoka scored a try in the 58th minute to give Japan a two-point lead after Ireland's Garry Ringrose and Rob Kearney scored the opening tries. Yu Tamura's conversion and fourth successful penalty sealed the win. Scotland recorded their first World Cup victory with a 34–0 win over Samoa in Kobe, with Samoan captain Jack Lam describing the ball as "a bar of soap." Three days later, Ireland defeated Russia 35–0 in Kobe, with five different players scoring tries. Jordi Murphy was substituted in the 27th minute due to a possible rib injury, adding to Irish back row pain after losing Jack Conan. Japan won 38–19 in Toyota with a 85th-minute try from Kotaro Matsushima securing a bonus point. Russia was defeated 61–0 by Scotland, with George Horne scoring a hat-trick, making Scotland the first team in World Cup history to not concede a point in two consecutive matches. A red card to Bundee Aki in the 29th minute reduced Ireland to 14 men, but they won 47–5 over Samoa in Fukuoka, with Johnny Sexton scoring two tries. The Japan–Scotland match was under threat due to Typhoon Hagibis, with the Scottish Rugby Union demanding legal action if cancelled. After an inspection confirmed the match could proceed, Japan won 28–21 with Kenki Fukuoka scoring two tries, becoming the first Tier 2 team to qualify since 2007, topping the pool while Ireland finished second. Pool B began with New Zealand defeating South Africa 23–13. New Zealand scored two tries in four minutes from George Bridge and Scott Barrett, leading 17–3 at half-time. Pieter-Steph du Toit scored a converted try to bring the score to 17–10, but two penalties from Richie Mo'unga and Beauden Barrett sealed the win. In Higashiōsaka, Italy conceded an early try to Namibia but won 25–0 with a bonus point. Italy earned a second bonus-point victory in Fukuoka, scoring seven tries in a 48–7 win over Canada. In Toyota, South Africa defeated Namibia 54–0, scoring nine tries while Namibia managed only a Cliven Loubser penalty in the 23rd minute. New Zealand won 63–0 over Canada at Ōita Stadium, with Brad Weber scoring his first two tries and the Barrett brothers (Jordie, Beauden, and Scott) each scoring a try, becoming the first trio of brothers to start for New Zealand. New Zealand then defeated Namibia 62–0 in Chōfu, with Sevu Reece, Ben Smith, and Anton Lienert-Brown scoring two tries in the second half after Namibia allowed only 24 points in the first half. South Africa defeated Italy 49–3 in Fukuroi, with Cheslin Kolbe scoring two tries. South Africa then beat Canada 66–7, with Cobus Reinach scoring the fastest hat-trick in World Cup history in 11 minutes. The final two matches of the group—New Zealand vs. Italy and Namibia vs. Canada—were cancelled due to Typhoon Hagibis. New Zealand finished top of the pool, South Africa second. Pool C began with Argentina recovering from a 17-point half-time deficit against France at Tokyo Stadium, only for France's Camille Lopez to score a drop goal in the 70th minute to win 23–21. In Sapporo, England won a bonus-point match over Tonga with two tries from Manu Tuilagi. England followed with a 38–0 victory over the United States, with Joe Cokanasiga scoring two tries; the match was marred by the first red card of the tournament, given to United States' John Quill for a shoulder charge to Owen Farrell's head. Argentina rebounded from their loss to France with a 28–12 win over Tonga in Higashiōsaka, scoring all their tries in the first 28 minutes, including a hat-trick from Julián Montoya, before Tonga scored two tries to reduce the margin to 16. After Typhoon Mitag nearly cancelled the match, France lost consistency and allowed the United States to stay in the game before three late tries in the second half secured a 33–9 win in Fukuoka. In Chōfu, England defeated Argentina 39–10, with Tomás Lavanini shown a red card for a high tackle on Owen Farrell's head, forcing Argentina to play with 14 men. France qualified with a two-point win over Tonga at Kumamoto Stadium, after conceding the first 17 points, with Sonatane Takulua and Mali Hingano scoring tries to close the gap to three points, before Romain Ntamack scored two penalties in eight minutes to secure the win. Argentina finished their campaign with a 47–17 victory over the United States in Kumagaya, with Joaquín Tuculet and Juan Cruz Mallia each scoring two tries, their first since 2003. After the England–France match was cancelled due to Typhoon Hagibis, Tonga ended their campaign with a 31–19 win over the United States, converting a match-winning try by Telusa Veainu and securing a bonus point. England finished top of the pool, France second. Pool D opened with Australia defeating Fiji 18–0 in Sapporo after Fiji led by two points at half-time, with Australia scoring four tries in the second half for a bonus point. Wales beat Georgia 43–14 at City of Toyota Stadium, leading 29–0 at half-time and 22–0 after three tries in the first half.

In the 2019 Rugby World Cup, matches were affected by Typhoon Hagibis, leading to the cancellation of the Pool B game between New Zealand and Italy and the Pool C game between England and France, which were declared 0–0 draws due to safety concerns for public transport and evacuation orders in Tokyo and Kamaishi. The Namibia–Canada match in Kamaishi was also cancelled, following a level 5 evacuation order, and recorded as a 0–0 draw; Canada stayed in Kamaishi to assist with cleanup, while Namibia interacted with fans in Miyako City. In contrast, the Wales–Uruguay and United States–Tonga matches proceeded as scheduled. Tonga ended their campaign with a 31–19 victory over the United States, with Telusa Veainu converting the match-winning try and securing a bonus point. In Kumagaya, Georgia defeated Uruguay 33–7, with a dominant second-half performance earning a bonus point. Australia beat Fiji 18–0 in Sapporo, scoring four tries in the second half for a bonus point, while Wales defeated Georgia 43–14, leading 29–0 at half-time. In Kamaishi, Fiji initially led against Uruguay before a try from Juan Manuel Cat brought them to 12–0 at half-time, but Uruguay won 45–10 over Georgia in a bonus-point victory due to Semi Radradra scoring two tries and setting up three more. Australia also beat Uruguay 35–0 at Ōita Stadium, with Tevita Kuridrani and Dane Haylett-Petty each scoring two tries. In a later match at Ōita, Wales won 29–17 over Fiji, with Josh Adams scoring two tries and Wales qualifying for the quarter-finals. Australia defeated Georgia 27–8 in Fukuroi, and Wales beat Uruguay 35–13 in Kumamoto to finish undefeated and secure a quarter-final spot. The knockout stage featured three single-elimination rounds, with extra time and sudden death periods used if needed, and a kicking competition if tied. England defeated Australia 40–16 in Ōita, with Jonny May scoring two tries and 18 turnovers by Australia, prompting Michael Cheika’s resignation. New Zealand beat Ireland 46–14 in Tokyo, with Aaron Smith scoring two tries and a penalty try. France defeated Wales 20–19 in a match where Sébastien Vahaamahina was sent off, and Wales won with a 74th-minute try. South Africa beat Japan 26–3, with Makazole Mapimpi scoring two tries. In the semi-finals, England defeated New Zealand 32–12, with Mapimpi and Cheslin Kolbe scoring tries, while South Africa beat Wales 32–12, with Damian de Allende and Josh Adams scoring tries. England started as favorites in the final but faced early setbacks, including Kyle Sinckler’s injury and injuries to South Africa’s Bongi Mbonambi and Lood de Jager, and were behind 12–6 at halftime due to handling errors. South Africa led 25–12 after Makazole Mapimpi’s try and 32–12 after Cheslin Kolbe’s try. The bronze medal was won by New Zealand in a convincing win over Wales. The tournament’s broadcasting was handled by International Games Broadcast Services (IGBS), using resources from Australia, France, New Zealand, South Africa, and the UK, with NHK covering selected games in 8K resolution. World Rugby streamed matches for unsold markets, Sport24 held in-flight broadcast rights, and in South Africa, SuperSport had rights, with SABC broadcasting the final via agreement with MultiChoice. The cancellations impacted pool standings, with France unable to claim top position and Italy eliminated from the tournament, while South Africa’s pool position remained unaffected due to their prior qualification.
